newsitem.title: GERMANY: French poll raises EMU doubts in Kohl coalition.
newsitem.headline: French poll raises EMU doubts in Kohl coalition.

text.p: Doubts are growing in Chancellor Kohl's coalition partner, the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), whether the European Union's planned single currency will be launched on time, a German newspaper said on Thursday.
The Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily quoted a member of the CSU state government in Bavaria as saying: "Since the French election we have agreed currency union must be postponed."

The report, released ahead of publication on Friday, posed a fresh embarrassment for Germany's beleaguered Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who leads the CSU, the sister party of Kohl's Christian Democrats.
Waigel was forced under pressure from within the coaliton this week to back down on plans to revalue gold reserves to fill budget gaps and help Germany to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).

The Sueddeutsche report also signalled trouble for Kohl, the euro's chief proponent. Although Germany is struggling to reduce its public debt and deficits in 1977 to meet target levels, he has insisted that Bonn will make the grade.

The report said the CSU state government and CSU members of the state assembly in Bavaria believed a single currency would be a "monetary death sentence" after new French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin suggested it could be launched with softer financial criteria.

A spokesman for Bavarian Premier Edmund Stoiber said in response to an inquiry that Stoiber saw only 50-50 chances of a punctual launch of the euro if France's new leaders met certain election campaign pledges.
During the campaign, Jospin said he wanted to renegotiate the EU's "stability pact" intended to limit budget deficits after the planned euro launch.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, France's new finance minister, has suggested that criteria in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union, including a requirement to cut public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, should be interpreted politically rather than in strict mathematical terms.

Stoiber, quoted by the Sueddeutsche, said softening the criteria could have disastrous consequences. "If people notice in the year 2005 that they have given up their currency too soon, we can really talk about a bomb in Europe," he said.
A spokesman for the CSU parliamentary group in the Bavarian state assembly said it had not yet reached a decision or resolution on the planned single currency.

The spokesman also denied the Sueddeutsche's report that the CSU group had severely criticised Waigel, saying that not a bad word had been spoken against the party leader at a group meeting on Wednesday.
